facts.fact: The biggest and most common problem on the pinion guide station is the shimming step, which causes operators to call for help approximately three to four times a day.

citation.transcript_quote: Our biggest problem was the shimmy... I would say maybe what, three, four times a day?

facts.fact: A wrong shim is effectively picked every time because operators are guessing without a reliable starting point, making first-attempt success rare.

citation.transcript_quote: Every time. Because you're kind of guessing in the dark.

facts.fact: The acceptable rolling-torque range for shimming on the P100 pinion guide is 14 to 19 (units as specified by engineering), and operators must try to reach that range on the first attempt.

citation.transcript_quote: especially with the range we have, 14 to 19, which is what they prefer.

facts.fact: The main issue with shimming is not knowing where to start to reach acceptable torque values; a recommended starting shim pack based on historical data would eliminate most wasted production time.

citation.transcript_quote: The main issue we have though is just knowing where to start to get acceptable values.

facts.fact: If the rolling torque value is out of range, the Unicom computer system will flag it and stop the operator from moving forward in the process, preventing an out-of-spec part from passing the station.

citation.transcript_quote: the computer will record the data, and if it's within range, it'll pass. If it's not within range, it doesn't pass.

facts.fact: Inverted bearing cup and cone assembly is one of the two most error-prone tasks on the station. Operators occasionally assemble the bearing cup and cones inverted. The press detects this immediately (it flags an out-of-range position), but once a part has been pressed in the wrong orientation it is incredibly difficult to remove — removal frequently damages the component and causes significant downtime. Line-engineer verified orientations (2026-07-14): the BIG bearing cup cod.248114A1 is assembled TIMKEN side facing UP, and the SMALL bearing cup cod.191440A1 is assembled TIMKEN side facing DOWN — the two cups use opposite conventions.

citation.transcript_quote: Operators occasionally assemble the bearing cup and cones inverted, and once a part is pressed incorrectly, it is incredibly difficult to remove.

facts.fact: Sometimes the bearing cup/cone presses far enough to pass the station test but is not seated correctly and will come back as a field failure; this is considered an engineering-level issue.

citation.transcript_quote: it'll press it, and I don't know if it's seated correctly or not... it passes our test, but it'll come back wrong.

facts.fact: CNH specified that a particular seal assembly (step 18 on the 600 series) must be kept together as a unit when installed; if it comes apart during assembly there is a risk the seal will leak in service, and this instruction is not documented in the written training material.

citation.transcript_quote: CNH told us... whenever you put this thing on, you want to keep it like this, assembled. Because if it comes apart... this seal won't be uh, it could leak in the future.

facts.fact: The pinion guide station runs four distinct procedures: 425 front axle, 425 rear axle, 600 front axle, and 600 rear axle.
The 600 series axle has more steps and different bearings and seals compared to the 425 series, making it a completely different assembly process.

citation.transcript_quote: It's completely different. Also the bearings are different. The seal is different.

facts.fact: The 600 series has the highest error rate of the four axle variants, primarily due to shimming complexity and the greater number of assembly steps.

citation.transcript_quote: The 600 series... The shimming and it has more steps, so it takes a little bit longer.

facts.fact: The target cycle time for the full pinion guide procedure is 30 minutes; the current average is approximately 40 minutes, largely due to shimming rework iterations.

citation.transcript_quote: 30 minutes... the whole procedure takes 40 minutes, right? Give or take.

facts.fact: When the torque target of 14–19 is proving difficult to reach, operators are now allowed to accept a lower value, which can reduce total cycle time to approximately 30 minutes.

citation.transcript_quote: since we can now go lower if it's giving us trouble, we might be able to reach 30 minutes.

facts.fact: A new operator requires approximately one full week of side-by-side training with an experienced operator or supervisor (Julio or Mateo) before working independently on the pinion guide station.

citation.transcript_quote: One week to train... I need to be one operator together with the new operator. Always assist them.

facts.fact: When onboarding a new technician, the first priorities are safety (parts are heavy) and learning to navigate the Unicom software and follow the step-by-step pictures before anything else.

citation.transcript_quote: how to use the software and how to not get hurt for sure for safety because these are heavy material.

facts.fact: Incorrect fixture and driver selection is one of the two most error-prone tasks on the station. Operators must match the fixture/driver code printed on the Unicom step screen to the code physically marked on the actual components. The correct drivers and fixtures are clearly detailed in the Work Instructions and regular operators know them well, but errors spike during cross-training or shift coverage — when a regular operator is on leave, a cross-trained backup is much more likely to select the wrong driver.

citation.transcript_quote: they need to match this one... there can be always some mistakes, you know.

facts.fact: Only one operator (Ethan) currently runs the pinion guide station on the single active shift; a substitute operator would not have the same shimming knowledge and is likely to make errors.

citation.transcript_quote: I'm the only guy that runs this station... if there was someone else new that is not him, then there's going to be some mistakes.

facts.fact: The 17-step procedure captured previously corresponds to the 425 rear axle; the 600 series procedure is a separate recipe with additional steps and is the model currently in production.

citation.transcript_quote: That's for a 425 rear series... The one that has 17 steps. You're doing that for the 425.

facts.fact: During shimming, operators generally know the direction of the required correction (too high or too low) but lack a reliable first-attempt starting value, which is the root cause of repeated iterations.

citation.transcript_quote: Usually know the issue, like I know the issue is like it's too low I have to hire or something like that.
